title: One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job
gist: Nick Indge reviews PhoneBox, an MIT-licensed, sideloaded Android app plus PC companion (v0.9.29) that turns an old phone or tablet into a secondary desk display with PC stats and a 131-widget catalog (Steam launcher, Home Assistant controls). Setup over USB took under a minute; downsides include an unsigned Windows app, broken wireless QR pairing in testing, and a recent high-severity security advisory for versions 0.9.23 and earlier.

insights.claim: PhoneBox, an MIT-licensed tool that turns old Android devices (Android 5.0+) into PC companion displays, installs via a single Linux terminal command that downloads the PC agent, verifies its checksum, optionally creates a systemd user service and installs the APK.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Illustrates the low-friction open-source tooling repurposing e-waste devices.

insights.claim: PhoneBox is not on the Google Play Store and must be sideloaded, requiring developer options and ADB over USB on the Android device.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Distribution outside Play limits mainstream reach to hobbyists.

insights.claim: The PhoneBox installer prints its own uninstall script, which the reviewer praises as rare at a time when removing apps often feels harder than installing them.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Easy uninstall is a trust signal for open-source tools with deep system access.

insights.claim: PhoneBox offers a catalog of 131 free widgets, including RSS feeds, timers, a Steam library launcher that starts PC games from the tablet, and Home Assistant smart-home controls, all configured from the PC's web interface.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Shows demand for secondary-display/home-dashboard use cases built on existing hardware.

insights.claim: PhoneBox's Windows companion app is currently unsigned, triggering SmartScreen warnings, and widget settings such as weather location must be changed in general preferences rather than within the widget.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Early-stage polish gaps typical of pre-1.0 open-source software.
insights.locator: While I didn’t have any major issues

insights.claim: PhoneBox's wireless pairing relies on the device's camera app scanning a QR code; the reviewer could never get it to work and the app has no built-in QR scanner, so the documented wireless path can dead-end.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Wireless-only users should expect setup friction.
insights.locator: Connecting the Android tablet with my PC

insights.claim: On November 20, 2026, PhoneBox published a high-severity security advisory for versions 0.9.23 and earlier that could let another app on the connected Android device execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC; it was fixed by v0.9.29.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Tools with deep host access carry real security risk; fast release cadence cuts both ways.
insights.locator: These minor gripes should be smoothed

insights.claim: The reviewer argues most people have an old phone or tablet lying unused and that PhoneBox gives such devices a genuinely useful second life as a zero-cost secondary display.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Device repurposing is a growing hobbyist niche aligned with anti-e-waste and anti-subscription sentiment.
insights.locator: As long as you’re part of the group
